card.title: National Highways Interconnectivity, India: 775 acres taken and 11,138 people affected across eleven corridors
card.place: Eleven national highway corridors in Bihar, Rajasthan, Odisha, Karnataka and West Bengal, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: National Highways Interconnectivity Improvement Project, P121185. Loan IBRD-83010 of US$500 million, approved 29 October 2013, effective 5 August 2014, mid-term review 12 May 2017. The closing date moved from 30 June 2019 to 30 September 2020. The loan was revised to US$307.74 million, all of which was disbursed. The road component was costed at US$1,106.4 million including US$468.05 million of Bank money, and came in at US$704.0 million including US$293.6 million of Bank money.

companies.name: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
companies.role: Borrower's implementing agency; state public works departments carried out the land acquisition. The completion report's data sheet names this ministry as the sole implementing agency, and presents the National Highways Authority of India as the implementing agency of a different programme and of a separate loan.
companies.desc: The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is a ministry of the Government of India; the Bank's completion report records that it was assigned the development of the 'non-core' national highways - those outside the National Highways Development Programme and Bharatmala, about 43 per cent of India's primary highway network.

card.community: The completion report of 29 June 2022 gives the scale: "The project impacted 775 acres of land, including 558 acres of private land, 6390 structures (including 451 CPRs) and 11,138 PAPs", CPRs being common property resources and PAPs project-affected people. It says that at closure "compensation and eligible assistance were duly paid to all PAPs in six of the 11 road corridors", and that the remaining five roads, in Bihar and West Bengal, were transferred to another Bank-funded project, the Green National Highway Corridors Project, where the pending resettlement plan actions would be closely monitored. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 February 2023 records that "disbursement of compensation to project-affected people (PAPs) were substantially delayed in several sections but by project closing, all 11,138 PAPs were compensated for land acquisition for the subprojects completed under the project". That statement is limited to the subprojects completed under the project, the same set as the completion report's six of eleven corridors, so the record holds a delay with no length, no date and no number of people attached to it. Both documents record that the land acquisition was mis-sized: the completion report says poor road designs led to inaccurate assessments of land acquisition needs, particularly on four roads in Bihar, and to variations in the numbers of those affected; the Evaluation Group says needs were inaccurately identified for four roads in Bihar because of inadequate road designs, and that road designs were revised to avoid bypasses that required land acquisition. The completion report says that although most of the land acquisition and resettlement for the project's 15 packages was completed on schedule, there were short but challenging sections on all corridors that were time consuming and led to implementation delays, and that although each state public works department had guaranteed land availability before the works began, in practice the entire land was not handed over. It rates social safeguards performance Moderately Satisfactory, and says the variable quality of work by non-governmental organisation consultants in some packages, with weak management of their contracts by the ministry, led to serious implementation delays. The project received 347 grievances and the completion report says all but one were resolved. Neither document gives a count of people relocated, and neither uses the words displaced or relocated. No village or neighbourhood is named.
card.displaced_note: Neither Bank document gives a count of people relocated by this project, and none is given here. What the completion report counts is 11,138 project-affected people, 775 acres of land taken of which 558 acres was private, and 6,390 structures affected including 451 common property resources, across eleven road corridors in five states. Project-affected people is a wider category than people moved: neither document separates people who lost a house from people who lost only land or a roadside pitch, and neither uses the words displaced or relocated anywhere. ICIJ puts displacement for this project at 23,016 and lists it in its confirmed-displacement table. ICIJ's own method page states what its figures count. It looked for what the Bank's documents call "Project-Affected People (PAP)" or "displaced people", searching those documents for the words "affected", "PAP" or "displaced". Where a document counted only households, it says it was necessary to look up the average number of family members per household. Because the documents do not all separate temporary impacts from permanent ones, it "decided to include all impacts", and it says the impact counted "can be as modest as losing less than 1 percent of their land or income". It drew mainly on resettlement action plans, which are written before the work is done, and looked to completion reports where no resettlement document existed. Its data stops at 31 December 2014. No figure matching 23,016 appears in the completion report or in the Independent Evaluation Group's review, and the documents do not explain the gap.
card.outcome: The resettlement is recorded as substantially done, with a delay that neither document quantifies. The completion report rates the project outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and the quality of monitoring Modest. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives the same three ratings and records no disagreement; it rates the quality of the completion report itself Modest. At closing 704 km of the 856 km planned in the three low-income states had been built, 82 per cent, and 212 km of the 215 km planned in the two middle-income states, 99 per cent; 155 km of civil works was unfinished and was moved to the Green National Highway Corridors Project, where 102 km of it had been completed by 31 March 2022.
card.confidence_note: The core account rests on one body of evidence: the World Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. No court record, press report or NGO field research about land acquisition under this project was found, and no Inspection Panel complaint. The findings set out here are the lender reporting on its own project. The completion report names the road sections completed under the project: Lasot-Karanli on NH11B and Pratapgarh-Padi on NH113 in Rajasthan, Anishabad-Aurangabad on NH98 in Bihar in two contract lots, Madhugiri-Chikaballapura-Mulgabal on NH234 in Karnataka, Purlia-Bankura on NH60A in West Bengal, and Bhojpur-Chattabar on NH200 and Nabarangpur-Koksara on NH201 in Odisha. It does not name the five sections transferred to the Green National Highway Corridors Project. Land disputes over highway widening in Bihar are documented elsewhere, including on NH77 and the Patna-Buxar road, but none of those records names a section financed by this loan, so none can be matched to it. The compensation delay the Evaluation Group records has no length, date, place or number of people attached to it in either document.

card.whole: By the World Bank's own count, average travel time on the project roads fell from 2 minutes a kilometre to 1.17 for cars and from 3 minutes to 1.7 for trucks, both better than target, and recorded road deaths fell 45 per cent from a baseline of 163 in 2009. Vehicle operating costs fell from Rs 8 to Rs 7.2 a kilometre for cars and from Rs 14 to Rs 12.6 for trucks, exactly the target figures; the Bank's Independent Evaluation Group says there is not enough evidence that those figures were cross-checked against other data. The completion report put the economic rate of return at 20.3 per cent for the eight road sections built, totalling 617.3 km, against 25.74 per cent estimated at appraisal for 1,200 km of road in eleven sections; it counts savings in vehicle operating costs, maintenance costs and travel time, and gives contract award and implementation delays, lower traffic and higher contract costs as the reasons for the drop. A road safety enforcement pilot whose budget was raised at restructuring from US$17.5 million to US$72.5 million spent US$3.2 million, and the Group concludes the pilot was not carried out; the Group also says the reported rise in the share of state roads in good and fair condition cannot be fully attributed to the project, because the classified network itself grew from 37,501 km to 87,995 km. All of these figures come from the World Bank's own documents; no independent check of them was found.
card.conditions: The loan triggered the Bank's policy on involuntary resettlement (OP 4.12) and its policy on indigenous peoples (OP 4.10), the latter because six of the corridors, in Odisha, Rajasthan and West Bengal, ran through areas where indigenous communities live. Corridor-specific resettlement action plans were prepared under a resettlement policy framework and published in India and at the Bank's InfoShop. Indigenous peoples development plans were written and their actions folded into the resettlement plans. The project required contractors to be handed 80 per cent of the land free of encumbrance within a set period, and gave grievance redressal committees a role in deciding eligibility where the plan's figures and what was found on the ground differed.
card.ecosystem: The completion report records that the design of subprojects was changed where forest land had to be diverted or where wildlife corridors were crossed. 775 acres of land was taken, 558 acres of it private, and 6,390 structures were affected, including 451 common property resources such as handpumps, some of which were relocated in consultation with communities and in coordination with the Integrated Tribal Development Agency.

card.title: Kenya's informal settlements upgrading project: six deaths the Bank was not told about
card.place: Majengo Talai in Kericho and Kwa Hakatsa and Mwatate in Mombasa, among KISIP settlements in 14 Kenyan counties

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-48730 and trust fund TF-18327 for the Kenya Informal Settlements Improvement Project (P113542). US$100 million of IDA approved 24 March 2011, effective 30 June 2011, revised to US$99.99 million, with US$93.29 million disbursed; the trust fund added US$8.3 million. Closing was extended twice, from 30 June 2016 to 31 May 2018 and then to 30 November 2019. Outcome was rated Satisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 14 August 2020).

lenders.name: Agence Francaise de Developpement (France)
lenders.role: US$45 million at appraisal, revised to US$39 million, with US$38.95 million disbursed (World Bank completion report).

lenders.name: Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sweden)
lenders.role: US$10 million at appraisal, revised to US$8.3 million and fully disbursed through trust fund TF-18327 (World Bank completion report).

card.community: The Bank's completion report says the infrastructure component had about 30,000 project-affected persons, roughly 2 per cent of its beneficiaries, and the tenure component about 18,000, roughly 14 per cent. It says all displacement was in-situ, inside the settlement, 'except for three settlements in Kericho and Mombasa (Kwa Hakatsa, Mwatate and Majengo Talai) where alternative land was required to resettle 82 households (328 PAPs) as they were living on environmentally fragile areas and could not be settled in-situ'. At project closing that move had not happened: land had been identified in Mombasa and the planning and resettlement process had begun, and two options for land were still being explored in Kericho. Of about 70 resettlement plans needed where tenure work caused displacement, about 61 had been cleared and about 40 had been implemented or nearly implemented when the completion report was written; no document found counts the people moved under them. The grievance system handled complaints at settlement, county and national level. Separately, the report records deaths on the project's works. Writing of 'the five fatality cases that were related to KISIP, which took place in 2015 and 2018', it says the issue was first identified from a review of a monthly progress report and that during an October 2018 mission, after the Bank asked the client to confirm all incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, 'the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred'. It says that although there was awareness at local level to report severe injuries and deaths to resident engineers, contractors and the police, 'there was a systemic failure of reporting to KISIP high level management and to the World Bank'.
card.killed_note: Six deaths in incidents involving the project's works or vehicles, in 2015 and 2018, recorded in the World Bank's completion report. The same paragraph refers to 'the five fatality cases that were related to KISIP' and then says the Bank team learned that six fatalities had occurred; it accounts for six cases, of which one was treated as resolved, three were in court, one was with an insurance company and one was still in discussion with the contractor. The Bank says the project team committed to enforcing the contracts until the affected families were compensated, with a deadline of the end of August 2020.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 7,952 for this project. The World Bank's completion report gives about 30,000 project-affected persons under the infrastructure component and about 18,000 under the tenure component, says all displacement was in-situ apart from 82 households (328 people) in three settlements who needed other land, and records that their resettlement had not been completed when the project closed. No document found counts anyone actually relocated, so no figure is entered here. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
card.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome satisfactory. At closing five of the six death cases were unresolved and the Bank said its supervision would continue until they were, and that the resettlement of the 82 households and the remaining resettlement plans, expected to be finished in September 2020, would also be supervised past closing. An action plan including a protocol for reporting incidents was put in place after the deaths came to light.
card.confidence_note: The deaths, the failure to report them to the Bank and the unfinished resettlement of the 82 households are all stated in the World Bank's own completion report, which also rates the project's overall outcome satisfactory. A search for independent reporting or litigation on harms under this project found none, so the Bank's own documents are the only source and the core harm rests on a single institution's account.

sources.title: Kenya - Informal Settlements Improvement Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Kenya - KE-Informal Settlements Improvement Proj: ICR Review

card.whole: By the Bank's own count the project upgraded 98.28 km of roads to bitumen standard against a target of 90 km, rehabilitated 120 km of footpaths, laid 59 km of sewers with 4,788 sewer connections, provided 8,739 new piped household water connections against a target of 7,306, and installed 21 ablution blocks, 11 water kiosks and 134 high-mast lights. Tenure security was recorded in 80 settlements against a target of 86, and about 7,300 title deeds were issued or sent to counties by closing. A survey the project commissioned put the number of people who benefited at 1,389,980 against a target of 1,030,000, and the number with improved tenure security at 125,525 against a revised target of 100,000 and an original target of 180,000; the project recorded 26,148 jobs on construction sites. An economic analysis done only at closing, covering 76 per cent of actual cost, counted travel time and vehicle cost savings, better access to jobs and services, fewer days lost to flooding, less property damage and health gains, and put the internal rate of return at 41.4 per cent for roads and drainage, 41.2 per cent for water and sanitation and 30 per cent for the floodlights; the Evaluation Group's data table gives one rate for that analysis, 38 per cent. Both the Bank and the Evaluation Group rated the outcome Satisfactory, and the Evaluation Group rated efficiency Substantial. Every figure comes from the lender or a survey it commissioned; no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered three policies: environmental assessment, cultural property and involuntary resettlement. A resettlement policy framework was disclosed on 26 November 2010 and re-disclosed after the mid-term review. Settlement-level resettlement action plans were required where planning, surveying or infrastructure work displaced people; about 70 were needed for the tenure component. The Bank also required that land titles not be released until land for the affected people had been identified and surveyed.
card.ecosystem: At project closing many of the drainage networks the project built were clogged with solid waste and wastewater, because residents and counties had not worked out how to collect waste and maintain the upgraded infrastructure.

card.title: Works Before Payment on the Aboadze to Volta 330 kV Line
card.place: Kwabenya, Ga East, Greater Accra, and the Aboadze to Volta 330 kV line through the Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions, Ghana

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-40920 of US$40.0 million to Ghana for the first phase of the Coastal Transmission Backbone subprogram of the West Africa Power Pool programme (WAPP APL 1, P075994), approved 30 June 2005, effective 1 November 2005 against a planned 29 November 2005, US$40.79 million disbursed. The completion report's footnote cites the Development Credit Agreement for Credit 4092-GH as dated 31 August 2005; neither Bank document gives a signing date. Original closing was 30 June 2009; actual closing was 30 June 2013. Environmental category B. The second phase (P094917) added Credit IDA-42130 of US$45 million to Ghana and Credit IDA-42140 of US$15 million to Benin, the Financing Agreements for which the report's footnote cites as dated 4 December 2007 (Credit 4213-GH) and 2 March 2007 (Credit 4214-BJ); the data sheet gives phase 2 approval on 29 June 2006 and effectiveness on 30 January 2008 for Ghana and 29 November 2007 for Benin; the two phases are covered by one completion report. Implementing agencies were the Volta River Authority and, after the 2009-2010 unbundling, the Ghana Grid Company Limited in Ghana, and the Communaute Electrique du Benin for Togo and Benin. The completion report of 28 February 2018 rated outcome Unsatisfactory, risk to development outcome High, Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory for Ghana and Unsatisfactory for Benin; the Independent Evaluation Group's review also rated outcome Unsatisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00004338, 28 February 2018; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 7 May 2018).

lenders.name: European Investment Bank, Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development
lenders.role: Co-financiers of the first phase named in the completion report's data sheet. The second phase was co-financed by the European Investment Bank, the African Development Bank and KfW (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018).

companies.name: Volta River Authority
companies.role: The Ghanaian state power authority that owned and built the line and prepared the resettlement action plan of December 2004 and its addendum. Its Real Estate Department wrote the addendum, valued the losses, paid the compensation and held the consultations with the quarry operators at Kwabenya. Transmission was transferred from it to the Ghana Grid Company Limited between 2009 and 2010 following the amendment of the Volta River Authority Act in 2005 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018; Resettlement Action Plan Addendum).
companies.desc: Ghana's state electricity generator, established in 1961 by an Act of Parliament and solely owned by the Government of Ghana. It combines hydro, thermal and solar plants, selling to the Electricity Company of Ghana (61% of market consumption) and directly to mines and industry, and for export to Communaute Electrique du Benin (for Togo and Benin) and SONABEL in Burkina Faso; its subsidiary NEDCo distributes electricity in northern Ghana.

companies.name: Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo)
companies.role: The state transmission company created out of the Volta River Authority, which took over the project and the transmission assets during 2009 and 2010 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018).
companies.desc: Ghana's electricity transmission utility and system operator, in its own report's words, incorporated in December 2006 and operational from August 2008, with the Government of Ghana as sole shareholder represented by the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Energy. The Energy Commission licenses it to operate the National Interconnected Transmission System exclusively, its stated mandate being 'to carry out the business of economic dispatch and transmission of electricity from facilities of wholesale suppliers to bulk customers or electricity distribution utilities in Ghana and West Africa without discrimination', and that mandate has been amended to allow commercial telecommunication services over its assets. It transmitted 23,551 GWh in 2023 against a peak demand of 3,618 MW, and its registered name was changed to 'Ghana Grid Company LTD.' with the Registrar of Companies' approval in August 2023.

card.community: The credit paid for a 330 kV transmission line from Aboadze in the west of Ghana to the Volta substation in the east, with substation works at Volta, Akosombo and Tema. The Volta River Authority's resettlement action plan of December 2004 covered a corridor 215 km long and 860 hectares in area, and recorded that 307 of the affected people gave the size of their household, which ranged from two to thirty-one people, a mean of between 5.1 and 8.6 people by district. The plan was then overtaken by the works. The Authority's addendum to it records that during construction the line had to be realigned at Amrahia, Amanfio, Teiman, Oyarifa, Kwabenya, Pokuase and Ayawaso in Greater Accra and at Kasoa and Mankesim in the Central Region, to avoid buildings that had gone up between the survey and the construction and so to avoid, in the addendum's words, huge compensation cost. The diversions lengthened the line from 215 km to 219.2 km, took the corridor from 860 hectares to 876, added eleven towers and created impacts on people the original consultation had never reached. The addendum's tally is 1,454 affected farms, 1,051 on the original line and 403 added by the diversions, and 410 buildings or structures actually condemned, 271 in Greater Accra, 136 in the Central Region and 3 in the Western Region. It says the bulk of those properties in Greater Accra were uncompleted and that the completed houses were mostly owner-occupied by relatives and dependants of the owners, that few tenants were found and none claimed, and that the period from consultation to relocation was at least three years. Separately from the property owners it counts 22 stone crackers at Kwabenya, who were excluded from the count of property owners because what they lost was the right to carry on an economic activity rather than a property right: quarry activity is not permitted inside a transmission line corridor. The addendum says most of these operators had already been moved to new areas nearby as a result of project activities and that their compensation was based on the temporary loss of income from the day of relocating and restarting, in the nature of a disturbance claim, even though they had no legal concessions or licences to operate; the entry for stone crackers in its schedule is GHc 18,968, to be paid by end of 2010. A cut-off date of 30 August 2008 was fixed for the line as a whole and a later one of 21 April 2010 agreed with the quarry operators at Kwabenya. The addendum records that the main concern of affected people in all the meetings was the timely payment of adequate compensation. The completion report says the Ghana component complied only partially with social requirements, that about 1,700 persons were affected, and that the mid-term review found the project was not in compliance with World Bank policies because construction started before compensation. The same report, rating borrower performance, calls this one of the minor failings detected at the mid-term review, 'the initiation of works without having compensated potentially affected persons', and says it was subsequently corrected. It states that by 2011 the Volta River Authority had fully settled outstanding compensation to all affected parties, including landowners and stone crackers, affected by the passage of the 330 kV line at Kwabenya.
card.killed_note: No deaths are recorded in the completion report, the Independent Evaluation Group's review or the resettlement documents.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,454 for this project, which it describes as an estimate of people displaced taken from World Bank documents. The figure 1,454 appears in the Volta River Authority's resettlement action plan addendum as the total number of affected farms, made up of 1,051 on the original line route and 403 added by the diversions, and not as a number of people. The completion report's own figure for people is 'about 1,700 persons were affected'. The addendum separately counts 410 buildings and structures actually condemned and 22 stone crackers at Kwabenya. No document found gives a count of people actually relocated.
card.outcome: The 330 kV lines and substations in Ghana were completed in 2009. The completion report says the Volta River Authority had fully settled outstanding compensation to all affected parties, including the landowners and stone crackers at Kwabenya, by 2011. The report rated the project's outcome Unsatisfactory, chiefly because the cross-border interconnections were not synchronised, and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed. The Ghana credit for the first phase closed on 30 June 2013 against an original date of 30 June 2009.
card.confidence_note: The finding that construction started before compensation is the Bank's own, recorded in its completion report as a mid-term review finding and repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The farm, structure and stone cracker counts, the diversions and the cut-off dates come from the Volta River Authority's own resettlement plan and addendum, published by the Bank. The lender and the implementing agency are therefore reporting on their own project and no independent account of this line's land acquisition was found. The completion report says that by 2011 all outstanding compensation had been fully settled, including for the stone crackers, and does not say how long any individual went unpaid, how many people were affected by the works that began before payment, or how many of the 410 condemned structures were lived in. The addendum's cover prints July 2010 in a shifted-glyph font that text extraction renders as nonsense, so its date is on the document and the catalogue date matches it, though the file name says April 2011. The 2004 plan is dated December 2004 in its own running header and February 2005 on its cover, and both are given. The addendum's table of affected houses does not add up: its district rows give 226, 16 and 1 in the column for the original number of affected people and its total row gives 43 for that column, while its columns for properties on the original line and properties affected by diversion, 292 and 118, do sum to the total of 410. The Independent Evaluation Group's review prints no date on its pages; the 7 May 2018 date is the Bank's catalogue field and is likewise unverified at document level. The same report records recurrent cash flow difficulties at the Communaute Electrique du Benin which delayed disbursement of money set aside to compensate people affected by the Ghana-Togo-Benin 330 kV line. That line sits under the second phase and a separate project number, its construction was financed by other lenders, and the report says the Benin component financed by this credit raised no social safeguard issue because it required no land acquisition or resettlement, so that finding is not carried here.

card.whole: In Ghana the project built the 330 kV Aboadze to Tema transmission line with its terminal substations, which the completion report says were commissioned in late 2009; upgraded switchgear and electromechanical equipment at the Aboadze switchyard and the Volta switching system, including circuit breakers, disconnect switches and protection and control facilities; installed telecommunication equipment for the third bulk supply point at the Accra East and Achimota substations; and upgraded the supervisory control and data acquisition and energy management systems, with the Akosombo and Kpong generating station reinforcements and the control centre completed by June 2013. A dam safety assessment and an emergency preparedness plan for the Akosombo, Kpong and Nangbeto stations were delivered, and power sector monitoring data for the regional member states were collected and disseminated. In Benin and Togo the new dispatching centre at the bi-national utility's headquarters and the backup centre in Cotonou were completed and operating at closing, and the dispatch modernisation, rehabilitation and emergency plan studies and a draft procedures manual were finished. Apart from those emergency plans and the monitoring data, every indicator was recorded at its baseline value or at nil, because the regional project was not commissioned by the closing date: no electricity was traded over the project's infrastructure, power losses along the interconnection links stayed at 6, 4, 8 and 4 per cent for the four utilities against a 2 per cent target for each, and the targets for outage reduction, detection and response time, delivered capacity and reactive power are all recorded as not achieved. Construction along the 330 kV line in Benin was unfinished when the Bank closed the financing of that activity on 30 June 2016, the report saying the Bank no longer had the resources for it and putting the remaining works at US$5 million to US$6 million, beyond the bi-national utility's own means; the cooperation agreement for the backbone is recorded as not in place. The Volta River Authority's control centre study was not completed and its training centre was not set up. At appraisal the Evaluation Group's review gives economic rates of return of 16 per cent for Ghana and 35 per cent for Benin on components accounting for 85 and 87 per cent of the appraisal estimates, with a net present value of US$64 million at a 10 per cent discount rate. At completion only the Ghana investments could be analysed, and the line was loaded at about 15 per cent of its 400 MW nominal capacity: the report's scenario at a 20 per cent load factor gives a benefit-cost ratio of 0.4 and a rate of return of 0.3 per cent, and a ratio above 1 needs the load factor at about 75 per cent. Gas through the West African Gas Pipeline did not materialise, so there was limited production to send over the line at its design capacity, and the aluminium smelter demand assumed at the Tema end did not materialise either. Both the report and the review rate efficiency Negligible and the outcome Unsatisfactory, and the report puts the risk to the development outcome High. All these figures are the lender's own; no check from outside the World Bank Group was found.
card.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered two safeguard policies, environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The Volta River Authority prepared an environmental management plan and put it in the bidding documents, and prepared a compensation and resettlement action plan dated December 2004 before implementation, later supplemented by an addendum covering the people the diversions affected. Under the plan, affected people were compensated at the Authority's valuation of crops, land and buildings, or, where they disagreed, at the figure set by an independent valuation the Authority paid for. The addendum states that the absence of title documents did not bar a claimant from payment once ownership could be ascertained and validated, that replacement cost was estimated with no depreciation deducted, and that household relocation expenses were factored in as a disturbance element. The Benin component triggered only the environmental assessment policy, because the works there were upgrades to control and communications hardware at existing substations and required no land acquisition or resettlement, which the report states at paragraph 44 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2018; Resettlement Action Plan Addendum).

card.title: Land and Property Taken Without Payment on an Assam Roads Package
card.place: Assam State Roads Project corridors, Assam, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-81360 for the Assam State Roads Project (P096018). US$320 million approved 13 March 2012. The completion report's financing table gives the loan's original and revised commitment as US$320,000,000 and US$280,777,402 disbursed, with the loan and the trust fund grant together committing US$321,750,000, revised to US$321,748,396, and US$282,525,798 disbursed; it puts the actual total project cost at US$282,525,798 against US$401,750,000 at appraisal. The Independent Evaluation Group's data sheet instead shows US$321,748,396.16 as the revised IBRD commitment and US$284,447,922.45 as the total project cost. Original closing 31 March 2018; restructured at level 2 on 29 March 2018 and closed 30 September 2019, 18 months late. Among the works the loan paid for was resettlement and rehabilitation assistance to project-affected people, and the Bank suspended work on one package until compensation was paid (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022128, 26 June 2020).

lenders.name: World Bank, trust fund
lenders.role: Grant TF-11446 alongside the loan: US$1,750,000 committed, revised to US$1,748,396, all of it disbursed (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020).

card.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated roads in Assam, 978 km by closing against a revised target of 1,000 km. At appraisal, social screening covered about 420 km of roads, with a census and socio-economic survey of the people in every structure and on all land within the corridor of impact for Phase I of the upgrading component. The assessment concluded that widening to two lanes would not need extensive resettlement because the work would mostly stay inside the existing right of way, and that about 80 per cent of the land needed was already available in stretches along the Phase I corridors. On one of the project's packages that broke down. The completion report states plainly that the project departed from the agreements reached under the Resettlement Action Plan and that the land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners. As a corrective measure, work on the affected package was suspended until the required processes were completed and the compensation funds were transferred. The completion report says compensation was otherwise largely paid on time, 'barring for one package'. The completion report records the remaining activity of compensation payment for land acquisition as settled, confirmed by the completion report mission. The Independent Evaluation Group repeats the episode and adds what the project team told it by email on 10 June 2020: that for the first three years no designated staff was involved in the land acquisition process, and that after the department strengthened its environment and social cell in the second half of the project 'all the compensation was fully paid, and all the land acquisition issues were amicably settled'. The project also could not obtain utilisation certificates for money spent on land acquisition and utility shifting by other state agencies, which the state met from its own funds, and the project's financial management rating was lowered to unsatisfactory for a year after it took two years to answer the Auditor General's inspection report. The policy on indigenous peoples was triggered at appraisal because some corridors were expected to pass through areas where indigenous communities had settled, and an Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared, but the completion report states the policy was never applied during implementation because the project did not pass through any major tribal settlements.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,891 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, and no document found says how many owners had their land and property taken without payment on the affected package.
card.outcome: The loan closed on 30 September 2019. Work on the package where land and property had been taken without payment was suspended until the compensation was transferred, and the completion report records the outstanding land acquisition compensation as settled. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 26 June 2020 repeats that there was one package where land and properties were acquired without compensation, and reports the project team's statement that all compensation was eventually paid.
card.confidence_note: The statement that land and properties were acquired without paying compensation to the owners is the Bank's own, in its completion report, and the suspension of the package is recorded there and repeated in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. Both accounts are the lender's, and no independent account was found. What is thin is everything around the episode: the documents do not name the package, the corridor, the district or the owners, do not say how many owners there were or how long they went unpaid, and do not say how much was eventually transferred or when. The closing statement that all compensation was paid is the project team's own, given to the evaluators by email rather than in a document.

card.whole: By the Bank's own count about 978 km of Assam's secondary road network was upgraded or rehabilitated against a revised target of 1,000 km, made up of about 248 km of widening and upgrading and about 730 km of pavement rehabilitation and strengthening. Average travel time fell 23 per cent on the upgraded roads and 27 per cent on the rehabilitated ones, against a target of 20 per cent; the completion report records all 978 km in good or fair condition at completion, and the review puts the share of Assam's whole secondary network in good or fair condition at 55 per cent against a target of 40 per cent. Rates of return at completion were 41.14 per cent for the upgrading roads and 25.79 per cent for the rehabilitation roads, against appraisal estimates of 45 per cent and 37.4 per cent. The completion report of 25 March 2020 rates efficiency Modest and the overall outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 26 June 2020 rates efficiency substantial and the outcome Satisfactory. Both are the lender reporting on its own project and no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project triggered six safeguard policies: environmental assessment, natural habitats, forests, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. The state government endorsed a resettlement and rehabilitation policy and entitlement matrix consistent with the Bank's policy; a resettlement policy framework guided later phases, and the action plans for the four first-phase upgrading works were disclosed in Assam on 19 July 2011 and by the Bank on 27 July 2011. A separate Indigenous Peoples Development Plan was prepared for the first and second phase roads. The Public Works Roads Department was to staff an Environment and Social Cell to carry the plans out and engage a local NGO to help; construction supervision consultants were to monitor that work and an independent consultant to evaluate it at mid-term and at the end (Project Appraisal Document, 17 February 2012). When land and property on one works package were taken without compensation, in breach of the agreed plan, work on that package was suspended until the process was completed and the compensation money transferred (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 March 2020).
